title: Constant-update working-set heaps on pointer machines
formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most \(C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))\)? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define \(\Gamma(x)=1+\) the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.

context_blocks.text: The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.

progress.text: Iacono states the pointer-model working-set/decrease-key problem at the Adaptive and Scalable Data Structures seminar.

The revised pointer-machine construction achieves O(1) amortized insertion, O(alpha(n)) amortized decrease-key, and O(1 + log Gamma(x)) worst-case extraction. Its introduction explicitly leaves removal of the inverse-Ackermann overhead open.

Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, and Tarjan obtain constant amortized decrease-key and stack-like extraction, with insertion bounded by any fixed iteration of log-star. This is not a constant insertion bound.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target. The required total-cost inequality must cover every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue; trading growing insertion time for constant decrease-key does not satisfy it.

sentences: A priority queue supports insertions, priority decreases and minimum extraction.
The extraction charge depends on the number of items inserted since the extracted item arrived.
The target combines this adaptive charge with constant amortized insertion and decrease-key.
Only pointer-machine operations and key comparisons are available.
The latest cited constructions retain a slowly growing factor in at least one update operation.
